name: sequoia-sq
why: A modern OpenPGP implementation with a CLI; the packet format it exposes is a worthwhile door, though it is a close call.

brief.what_it_is: sq is the command-line frontend for Sequoia, a Rust implementation of OpenPGP, installed as the executable 'sq'. It covers common OpenPGP tasks: encrypt and decrypt messages, sign and verify messages or detached signatures, download a file and check its signature, generate and manipulate keys and certificates, query keyrings, look up or publish certs over the network, and inspect any OpenPGP data (similar to file(1)). Inputs are files, stdin, URLs or keyrings, in binary or ASCII-armored form, and the tool handles armor automatically. Output is ASCII-armored by default. The homepage says Sequoia is a new OpenPGP library focused on safety and correctness and written in a memory-safe language.
brief.why_it_exists: The homepage frames Sequoia as 'a new OpenPGP Library' with a focus on safety and correctness, and says improving the security of OpenPGP users 'requires more than a new implementation', so the project is also improving the surrounding ecosystem. The sq manual pitches the CLI as a tool that makes OpenPGP usable for ordinary tasks and offers a Web of Trust authentication model as an alternative to X.509 certificate authorities.
brief.how_it_works: Commands are grouped into subcommands (encrypt, decrypt, sign, verify, download, inspect, cert, key, pki, network, keyring, packet, config, toc, version). The interface is not fully stateless: it uses a default certificate store under $HOME/.local/share/pgp.cert.d and a key store server under $HOME/.local/share/sequoia/keystore, which sq starts if none is running. Verification succeeds only if there are no bad signatures and the count of good ones meets the --signatures threshold. The CLI is versioned and --cli-version can pin an interface version. The --time and --policy-as-of flags let you verify or inspect data as of a past reference time.

commands_seen.context: Encrypts document.txt for a recipient looked up by email address and signs it with a second key identified by email.
Decrypts ciphertext.pgp using a secret key file as the recipient key.
Decrypts and also checks any signatures against the supplied signer certificate file. Verification only passes if signatures are good.
Creates a detached signature for document.txt in document.txt.sig. The manual wraps this line; it is joined here.
Verifies a detached signature document.sig against document.txt.
Verifies a signed message as of June 19, 2024 at midnight UTC, using the reference time flag.
Verifies a message under the cryptographic policy as of January 1, 2007. The manual warns that this should only be used when you are confident the message has not been tampered with.
Downloads the Debian 12 checksum file and its signature, checks the signature against the given signer fingerprint, and writes the output. The manual wraps this line; it is joined here.
Shows how a certificate looked on July 21, 2013, by inspecting it at a past reference time.
Describes an encrypted message in human-readable form, like file(1) does for other formats.

brief.install_notes: The GitLab README is only a one-line description plus the license, with no install steps seen, so no build or runtime requirements were visible beyond what the manual says. Default config lives at $HOME/.config/sequoia/sq/config.toml, and a config template can be created with sq config. A key store server starts automatically on first use unless --key-store=none is passed. The manual says sq uses the 'default' home unless --home is set, and --home or SEQUOIA_HOME can isolate its data. Nothing Homebrew-specific was seen.
brief.standout: Unlike many OpenPGP tools, sq treats time as a first-class input: --time and --policy-as-of let you inspect or verify data as of any past date, and sq download fetches and authenticates a file in one step. The manual also says sq packet dump is useful as a learning tool for the OpenPGP packet format, which matches the scout's note that the packet layer is the most interesting door, though this is a close call since the other features are more conventional.
brief.status: maintained. The homepage news includes posts dated January 12, 2026 and February 3, 2026. The manual is for version 1.5.0 and says the CLI interface is at version 1.5.0. The GitLab project was created February 17, 2023. No release date for 1.5.0 or last-commit date was visible.
brief.caveats: A January 2026 post on the Sequoia blog responds to a 39C3 talk ('To sign or not to sign') that reported vulnerabilities in GnuPG, Sequoia, age and minisign. The author argues the attack on sq came from a literal translation of gpg commands into sq commands, with the user ignoring sq's output, and says the ecosystem still needs to improve. Verification output is withheld: when a failed check writes to stdout, the last 25 MiB are withheld. The license is shown on GitLab as 'GNU Library General Public License v2 only', which is the LGPL-2.0-only name. The README is thin and the detailed docs live in the manual and the book, which I did not fetch. The homepage is mostly marketing and testimonials.
quotes: A command-line frontend for Sequoia, an implementation of OpenPGP.
sq packet dump may be helpful to a wider audience both to provide valuable information in bug reports to OpenPGP-related software, and as a learning tool.
A command line application exposing a useful set of OpenPGP functionality for common tasks.
fetch_log: https://sequoia-pgp.org: worked, but it is mostly marketing and testimonials with no sq command lines, so I followed to the repository.
https://gitlab.com/sequoia-pgp/sequoia-sq: worked, but the README is only a one-line description and the license, so I followed to the manual.

judge.reason: Beyond routine encryption, sq makes OpenPGP packets inspectable and lets you verify certificates and signatures under historical time and policy rules.

entry.title: sq (Sequoia-PGP)
entry.tldr: A Rust OpenPGP command-line tool that encrypts, signs and verifies, and can inspect keys and messages as of any past date.
entry.deeper_look:
sq is the command-line frontend for Sequoia, a Rust implementation of OpenPGP. It covers the usual tasks: encrypt and decrypt, sign and verify (including detached signatures), generate and manage keys and certificates, query keyrings, and look up or publish certificates over the network. Armor is handled automatically, and output is ASCII-armored by default.

The homepage describes Sequoia as a new OpenPGP library focused on safety and correctness, and says that improving the security of OpenPGP users "requires more than a new implementation". The sq manual also pitches a Web of Trust model as an alternative to X.509 certificate authorities.

The interesting door is inspection. `sq inspect` describes any OpenPGP data in human-readable form, much like file(1) does for other formats. Beneath it, `sq packet dump` shows the packet structure, and the manual says it may be useful "as a learning tool". Time is also a real input: `--time` and `--policy-as-of` let you verify or inspect data as it would have looked on a past date, under the cryptographic policy of that era.

sq is not fully stateless. It uses a certificate store under `$HOME/.local/share/pgp.cert.d` and starts a key store server on first use unless you pass `--key-store=none`. `--home` or `SEQUOIA_HOME` isolates its data, which is a good idea while experimenting.
entry.install:
brew install sequoia-sq
# Optional: keep experiments away from your real data
# export SEQUOIA_HOME=$(mktemp -d)

try_this.what_happens: Lists the subcommands: encrypt, decrypt, sign, verify, download, inspect, cert, key, pki, network, keyring, packet and more.
Describes an OpenPGP message or certificate in human-readable form, like file(1) does for other formats.
Shows how a certificate looked on a past date, such as July 21, 2013.

entry.whats_unique: sq treats time as a first-class input, so you can inspect or verify data as of any past date and policy. `sq download` also fetches a file and authenticates it against a signer fingerprint in one step.
entry.caveats: A January 2026 Sequoia blog post answers a 39C3 talk that reported vulnerabilities in several tools including sq, blaming literal gpg-to-sq command translation and ignored output; the README is also thin, so the manual is where the real docs are.
